subtype: Approach: overnight resolution to change everything [Pitfall]
passage: Note, Sunday night. After Vaibhav's bad chemistry result on Friday, I watched him write a new timetable and pin it above the desk: lights out at nine at night, up at four in the morning, from the very next day. No half-measures. On Monday the alarm rang at four and he was up, grey-faced, and fell asleep on the sofa by five in the afternoon. On Tuesday the alarm rang and he did not get up. He dropped the timetable in the bin and said, "I can't even do this." What I did: I took it out of the bin, told him the plan was too big for anyone and not a sign of weakness, and asked if we could pick one small change together. He shrugged but sat down with me. We chose one thing: the same wake time every day. - Hansa

qa.q: What bedtime and wake time did Vaibhav pin above the desk?
qa.a: Vaibhav pinned lights out at nine at night and up at four in the morning.

qa.q: How did Vaibhav feel when saying 'I can't even do this'?
qa.a: Vaibhav felt defeated and like a failure, after the plan collapsed in two days on top of a bad result.

qa.q: What could Vaibhav try instead of an overnight jump, and why?
qa.a: Vaibhav could fix one wake time and move bedtime earlier in small steps, because gradual changes are easier to keep than an unrealistic leap.

qa.q: How does Hansa see the failed timetable?
qa.a: Hansa sees a plan that was too big for anyone, and not a sign of weakness, which is why Hansa rescues it from the bin and offers a smaller start.

grounding: After a bad exam, the student resolves to sleep at 9 pm and wake at 4 am from tomorrow, and the unrealistic jump fails in two days and leaves the student feeling like a failure.
